bricks.title: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract

items.why: Nares: external aperture where inhaled air first enters the nasal cavity
Vestibule (keratinized), respiratory region (humidifies), olfactory region (CN I)

questions.q: Which region of the nasal cavity contains the olfactory receptor neurons?
questions.explain: The olfactory region is lined by specialized mucosa containing olfactory receptor neurons for smell (CN I).

questions.q: Which nasal cavity region is lined by keratinized stratified epithelium?
questions.explain: The vestibule, just inside the nares, is lined by keratinized stratified epithelium; the respiratory region is highly vascular and humidifies air.

items.why: Septum: ethmoid + vomer + anterior cartilage; Kiesselbach plexus on anterior septum

questions.q: Which two bones form the bony part of the nasal septum?
questions.explain: The septum has two bony components (ethmoid and vomer) plus a cartilaginous part that occupies most of the anterior septum.

questions.q: A child has a common anterior nosebleed after nose-picking. The bleeding most likely arises from which vascular network on the anterior septum?
questions.explain: Common anterior epistaxis arises from the Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior nasal septum, formed by branches of the internal and external carotids.

items.why: Conchae on lateral wall: surface area to warm/humidify air

questions.q: What is the main function of the nasal conchae?
questions.explain: The mucosa-lined conchae on the lateral wall provide a large surface area for humidification and warming of inspired air.

items.why: Meatuses: inferior = nasolacrimal duct; middle = maxillary/frontal/ant ethmoid; superior = post ethmoid

questions.q: Into which meatus do the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain?
questions.explain: The middle meatus (under the middle concha) drains the maxillary, frontal, and anterior and middle ethmoid sinuses.

questions.q: The superior meatus provides drainage for which sinus?
questions.explain: The superior meatus drains the posterior ethmoid sinuses; most other sinus ostia open into the middle meatus.

items.why: Nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the inferior meatus

questions.q: Where does the nasolacrimal duct open into the nasal cavity?
questions.explain: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the medial eye into the inferior meatus, which is why crying gives you a runny nose.

items.why: Bones of nasal cavity: maxilla floor, frontal anterior roof, sphenoid posterior roof

questions.q: Which bone forms the floor and part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity?
questions.explain: The maxilla forms the floor and a portion of the lateral wall; the palatine bone also contributes to the floor.

questions.q: Which bone forms the posterior portion of the nasal cavity roof?
questions.explain: The sphenoid forms the posterior roof, the frontal bone the anterior roof, and the ethmoid contributes to the roof and walls.

items.why: Sphenopalatine a.: major artery of Woodruff plexus (posterior epistaxis)

questions.q: A patient has a severe posterior nosebleed from the Woodruff plexus. Which artery is a major contributor to this plexus?
questions.explain: Woodruff's plexus in the posterior nasal cavity is formed mainly by the sphenopalatine and ascending pharyngeal arteries; posterior bleeds are less common but often more severe.

items.why: Frontal sinus: drains to middle meatus; ophthalmic a. (ICA); V1

questions.q: The frontal sinus receives its blood supply from branches of which artery?
questions.explain: The frontal and ethmoid sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic artery, which arises from the internal carotid.

items.why: Maxillary sinus: largest, high medial ostium to middle meatus; maxillary a.; V2

questions.q: Why does the maxillary sinus drain poorly and become easily obstructed?
choices: Its ostium is high on the medial wall
It drains into the inferior meatus
It has no direct ostium of its own
questions.explain: The maxillary sinus is the largest sinus, and because its ostium is located high on its medial wall, drainage is less efficient and easily impaired.

questions.q: Sensory innervation of the maxillary sinus comes from which nerve?
questions.explain: The maxillary sinus is innervated by branches of the maxillary nerve (V2); the frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses by the ophthalmic nerve (V1).

questions.q: A patient with a week-long cold now has fever and tenderness to percussion over the left cheek. Which sinus is most likely infected?
questions.explain: Cheek pressure and tenderness point to the maxillary sinus, whose middle-meatus drainage is easily obstructed by mucosal swelling, producing acute sinusitis.

items.why: Ethmoid sinuses: anterior/middle to middle meatus, posterior to superior meatus; ophthalmic a.; V1

questions.q: The ethmoid sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic artery. The ophthalmic artery arises from which vessel?
questions.explain: The frontal and ethmoid sinuses receive blood from the ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery.

items.why: Sphenoid sinus: drains to sphenoethmoidal recess; maxillary a.; V1

questions.q: The sphenoid sinus drains into which space?
questions.explain: The sphenoethmoidal recess, the fourth drainage channel above the superior concha, drains the sphenoid (and posterior ethmoid) sinuses.

questions.q: Which artery supplies the sphenoid sinus?
questions.explain: The sphenoid and maxillary sinuses are supplied by branches of the maxillary artery, from the external carotid.

items.why: Maxillary a. (from ECA): supplies maxillary and sphenoid sinuses

questions.q: The maxillary artery, which supplies the maxillary and sphenoid sinuses, is a branch of which artery?
questions.explain: The maxillary artery stems from the external carotid artery and supplies the sphenoid and maxillary sinuses.

items.why: ECA: ascending pharyngeal, facial, superior thyroid branches supply pharynx/larynx

questions.q: The ascending pharyngeal artery, the primary supply of the nasopharynx, is a branch of which artery?
questions.explain: Branches of the external carotid supply the nasopharynx, with the ascending pharyngeal artery as the primary supply.

items.why: ICA: ophthalmic a. to frontal/ethmoid sinuses; contributes to Kiesselbach

questions.q: Branches of which artery contribute to the Kiesselbach plexus together with the external carotid?
questions.explain: The Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum is an anastomosis of branches originating from both the internal and external carotid arteries.

items.why: Nasopharynx: air only; soft palate inferior border; ascending pharyngeal a.; retropharyngeal nodes

questions.q: Which part of the pharynx normally carries only air and not food?
questions.explain: All three parts conduct air, but only the oropharynx and laryngopharynx accommodate food; the nasopharynx normally carries air only.

questions.q: Lymph from the nasopharynx drains primarily to which nodes before the deep cervical nodes?
questions.explain: Nasopharyngeal lymph drains primarily to the retropharyngeal nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein.

items.why: Adenoids: lymphatic tissue on posterior nasopharyngeal wall

questions.q: The pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) are located on which wall of which region?
questions.explain: The pharyngeal tonsils sit on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx; like the palatine tonsils, they can become inflamed (tonsillitis).

items.why: Pharyngotympanic tube: nasopharynx to middle ear, equalizes pressure; occlusion -> otitis media

questions.q: What is the function of the pharyngotympanic (eustachian) tube?
questions.explain: The pharyngotympanic tube links the nasopharynx to the middle ear, equalizing middle-ear pressure with atmospheric pressure.

questions.q: A nasopharyngeal mass occludes the opening of this tube. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explain: Occlusion of the pharyngotympanic tube opening impedes middle-ear drainage into the nasopharynx, causing recurrent middle ear swelling and infection (otitis media).

items.why: Oropharynx: uvula to hyoid; facial a. branches; CN IX

questions.q: The oropharynx extends inferiorly to the level of which structure?
questions.explain: The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity and extends from the uvula to the hyoid bone.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the oropharynx?
questions.explain: The oropharynx receives its innervation from branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

items.why: Facial a.: main oropharyngeal supply via tonsillar and ascending palatine aa.

questions.q: Which artery provides the main arterial supply of the oropharynx via its tonsillar and ascending palatine branches?
questions.explain: The oropharynx is supplied mainly by branches of the facial artery, including the tonsillar and ascending palatine arteries.

items.why: Palatine tonsils: lymphatic tissue in the oropharynx; tonsillitis

questions.q: The palatine tonsils, commonly infected in tonsillitis, are located in which part of the pharynx?
questions.explain: The palatine tonsils are collections of lymphatic tissue on the left and right of the oropharynx, seen on a routine throat exam.

items.why: Uvula: with soft palate closes nasopharynx during swallowing

questions.q: During swallowing, the uvula works with the soft palate to do what?
questions.explain: The uvula collaborates with the soft palate to close the connection to the nasopharynx, preventing food from moving up into the nose.

items.why: Laryngopharynx: epiglottis to cricoid -> esophagus; CN IX + X via pharyngeal plexus

questions.q: The laryngopharynx continues into the esophagus at the inferior border of which structure?
questions.explain: The laryngopharynx extends from the superior border of the epiglottis to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, where it continues into the esophagus.

questions.q: Motor and sensory innervation of the laryngopharynx comes from which nerves?
questions.explain: Both motor and sensory supply to the laryngopharynx arise from the glossopharyngeal (CN IX) and vagus (CN X) nerves via the pharyngeal plexus.

items.why: Epiglottis: closes larynx in swallowing; internal branch of SLN sensory

questions.q: What is the function of the epiglottis?
questions.explain: The epiglottis is a flap of cartilage that closes the larynx when swallowing to prevent aspiration of food into the airways.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the epiglottis and laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds?
questions.explain: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X) gives sensation above the vocal folds, triggering protective cough reflexes.

items.why: Pyriform fossae beside laryngeal inlet; trap food/fish bones

questions.q: A patient feels a fish bone stuck in the throat. Lodging in which pear-shaped recess beside the laryngeal inlet is classic?
questions.explain: The pyriform fossae are recesses adjacent to the laryngeal inlet in the laryngopharynx; food such as fish bones can get trapped there.

items.why: Superior/middle/inferior constrictors guide food; dysfunction -> Zenker diverticulum

questions.q: Spasm or poor relaxation of the pharyngeal constrictors raising pharyngeal pressure can produce which lesion?
questions.explain: Spasm or decreased relaxation of these muscles increases pharyngeal pressure and causes herniation at the laryngopharynx: a Zenker diverticulum (pharyngeal pouch).

items.why: CN IX: oropharynx innervation; pharyngeal plexus with CN X

questions.q: Which cranial nerve, along with the vagus, contributes to the pharyngeal plexus supplying nasopharyngeal mucosa?
questions.explain: The pharyngeal plexus has contributions from CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and CN X (vagus); CN IX alone innervates the oropharynx.

items.why: Vagus: superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves; pharyngeal plexus

questions.q: The superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves are branches of which cranial nerve?
questions.explain: Both the superior laryngeal and the recurrent laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus nerve, supplying the laryngeal muscles for phonation.

items.why: Supraglottis, glottis (vocal cords), subglottis (to trachea)

questions.q: Which region of the larynx contains the true vocal cords?
questions.explain: The supraglottis runs from the epiglottis to just above the cords, the glottis contains the vocal cords, and the subglottis extends to the trachea.

items.why: Hyoid: inferior limit of oropharynx; supra/infrahyoid muscles

questions.q: The epiglottis is attached to the thyroid cartilage and to which other structure?
questions.explain: The epiglottis is attached to the hyoid bone and to the thyroid cartilage (via the thyroepiglottic ligament).

items.why: Thyroid cartilage: unpaired, anterior larynx; laryngeal prominence

questions.q: Which unpaired laryngeal cartilage forms the anterior surface of the larynx?
questions.explain: The thyroid cartilage lies on the anterior surface of the larynx; its laryngeal prominence is the Adam's apple.

items.why: Laryngeal prominence = Adam's apple, part of thyroid cartilage

questions.q: The laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) is part of which cartilage?
questions.explain: The laryngeal prominence of the thyroid cartilage is visible as the Adam's apple in most males.

items.why: Cricoid: encircles subglottis; laryngopharynx->esophagus and trachea begin at its level

questions.q: Which cartilage encircles the subglottis?
questions.explain: The cricoid cartilage, one of the three unpaired cartilages, encircles the subglottis; the trachea begins at its inferior border.

items.why: Cricothyroid membrane interconnects cricoid and thyroid cartilages

questions.q: The cricothyroid membrane connects which two structures?
questions.explain: The cricoid and thyroid cartilages are stabilized and interconnected by the cricothyroid membrane; the thyrohyoid membrane links thyroid cartilage to hyoid.

items.why: Paired arytenoids: vocal cords attach

questions.q: To which paired laryngeal cartilage do the vocal cords attach?
questions.explain: The paired arytenoid cartilages are where the vocal cords attach; the corniculate and cuneiform are the other paired cartilages.

items.why: True cords vibrate in phonation; false/vestibular folds; ventricle between; testosterone

questions.q: What is the small lateral recess between the vestibular folds and the true vocal folds called?
questions.explain: The laryngeal ventricle lies between the vestibular (false) and true vocal folds and contains mucous glands that lubricate the cords.

questions.q: Why do males develop a lower-pitched voice at puberty?
choices: The larynx descends below the cricoid
Testosterone thickens and lengthens the cords
questions.explain: Vocal cord development is affected by testosterone during puberty, which causes thickening and elongation and a lower-pitched voice.

items.why: Posterior cricoarytenoid: the only abductor of the vocal folds

questions.q: Which is the only laryngeal muscle that abducts the vocal folds?
questions.explain: The posterior cricoarytenoids are the only muscles that abduct the vocal folds, making them the main intrinsic muscle supporting respiration.

items.why: Cricothyroid: tenses cords for pitch; external branch of SLN

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle?
questions.explain: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords to control pitch.

questions.q: What is the main action of the cricothyroid muscle?
questions.explain: Voice pitch is controlled mainly by the cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords; the posterior cricoarytenoid is the abductor.

items.why: Transverse/oblique arytenoid: intrinsic muscle controlling phonation

questions.q: The transverse and oblique arytenoid muscles are classified as which kind of laryngeal muscle?
questions.explain: Intrinsic muscles have origins and insertions within the larynx and control the cords; they include the transverse and oblique arytenoids.

items.why: Thyroarytenoid: intrinsic muscle controlling phonation
SLN (CN X): internal = sensation above folds/cough; external = cricothyroid

questions.q: Food touching the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds triggers a cough. Which nerve carries this sensation?
questions.explain: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensation above the vocal folds, letting the larynx detect food and trigger protective reflexes.

items.why: RLNs: phonation muscles; left loops under aortic arch; neck surgery -> hoarseness

questions.q: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around which structure?
questions.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the aortic arch before ascending to the larynx.

questions.q: After thyroid surgery, a patient has a hoarse voice. Which nerve was most likely damaged?
questions.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply the phonation muscles and are easily damaged during neck surgery, which can lead to hoarseness.

items.why: Suprahyoids (digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid) elevate the larynx

questions.q: What action do the suprahyoid muscles have on the larynx?
questions.explain: The suprahyoid group (digastric, stylohyoid, geniohyoid, mylohyoid) are extrinsic muscles that elevate the larynx.

items.why: Infrahyoids (sternothyroid, omohyoid, thyrohyoid, sternohyoid) depress the larynx

questions.q: Which muscle is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the larynx?
questions.explain: The infrahyoid muscles (sternothyroid, omohyoid, thyrohyoid, sternohyoid) lie below the hyoid and depress the larynx.

bricks.title: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract

items.why: Trachea: cricoid to T5; U-shaped anterior/lateral rings; posterior trachealis

questions.q: At what vertebral level does the trachea bifurcate into the primary bronchi?
questions.explain: The trachea begins at the cricoid cartilage, runs about 11 cm, and bifurcates at the fifth thoracic vertebra, at the carina.

questions.q: What lies in the posterior wall of the trachea, where the cartilage rings are absent?
questions.explain: U-shaped cartilage rings cover the anterior and lateral trachea; the posterior wall is a fibrous membrane surrounding the trachealis muscle, against the esophagus.

items.why: Carina: tracheal bifurcation at T5

questions.q: At the carina, the trachea divides into which airways?
questions.explain: At the carina the trachea branches into the right and left primary (main) bronchi.

items.why: Primary bronchi: right wider and more vertical -> foreign bodies

questions.q: A 3-year-old aspirates a bead. Where is it most likely to lodge?
questions.explain: Foreign bodies usually lodge in the right main bronchus, which is wider and more vertical than the left.

questions.q: Why does the left main bronchus branch from the trachea at a wider angle than the right?
choices: The aortic arch is on the right
The heart sits on the left side
The left lung has three lobes
The esophagus lies on the left
questions.explain: The left main bronchus is narrower and branches at a wider angle because the heart sits on the left side of the chest.

items.why: Lobar bronchi: 3 right, 2 left; plate cartilage, can collapse in forced expiration

questions.q: How many secondary (lobar) bronchi does the left lung have?
questions.explain: There is one lobar bronchus per lobe: the right lung has three lobes and lobar bronchi, the left lung two.

items.why: Segmental bronchi supply bronchopulmonary segments (surgically resectable)

questions.q: Each bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by its own pulmonary artery branch and which airway?
questions.explain: A bronchopulmonary segment is a discrete unit supplied by its own segmental bronchus and pulmonary artery branch.

questions.q: Why is the bronchopulmonary segment clinically important?
choices: It can be resected without harming neighbors
It is the site of all gas exchange
It is supplied by the bronchial artery alone
It lacks any surrounding connective tissue
questions.explain: The segment is the smallest functionally independent region of the lung, separated by connective tissue, so it can be surgically resected without affecting neighboring segments.

items.why: Apex above 1st rib into neck; base on diaphragm; root via hilum

questions.q: Superiorly, the apex of each lung extends to what level?
choices: Root of the neck, above the first rib
Level of the jugular notch only
Level of the second costal cartilage anteriorly
questions.explain: Superiorly each lung extends into the root of the neck just above the first rib; inferiorly the base rests on the diaphragm.

questions.q: Which structure passes through the hilum in the root of the lung?
questions.explain: The root, running through the hilum, contains the primary bronchus, pulmonary artery and vein, pulmonary plexus, and hilar lymphatics.

items.why: Right lung: superior, middle, inferior lobes
Left lung: superior and inferior lobes
Right lung: horizontal and oblique fissures

questions.q: In the right lung, the horizontal fissure separates the superior lobe from which lobe?
questions.explain: The horizontal fissure separates the right superior lobe from the middle lobe; the oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe.

items.why: Left lung: oblique fissure between superior and inferior lobes

questions.q: Which fissure separates the superior and inferior lobes of the left lung?
questions.explain: The left lung has only an oblique fissure, separating its superior and inferior lobes; it lacks a horizontal fissure.

items.why: Cardiac notch: deflection of anterior left lung accommodating heart

questions.q: What structure does the cardiac notch of the left lung accommodate?
questions.explain: The cardiac notch is a deflection of the anterior surface of the left lung that accommodates the heart.

items.why: Lingula: extension of left superior lobe, analog of right middle lobe

questions.q: The lingula is part of which lobe of the left lung?
questions.explain: The lingula ('little tongue') is an extension of the left superior lobe and is the analogue of the right middle lobe.

items.why: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right heart

questions.q: What kind of blood do the pulmonary arteries carry?
choices: Oxygenated blood returning to the left atrium
Mixed blood from the azygos system
Deoxygenated blood from the right heart
questions.explain: In the pulmonary circulation, deoxygenated blood moves from the right heart to the lungs via the pulmonary trunk and arteries.

items.why: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left heart

questions.q: Oxygenated blood returns from the pulmonary capillaries to the heart via which vessels?
questions.explain: After gas exchange in the pulmonary capillaries, oxygenated blood returns to the left heart via the pulmonary veins.

items.why: Bronchial arteries (thoracic aorta): oxygenated blood for lung metabolism

questions.q: What is the main function of the bronchial arteries?
choices: Carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange
Drain the airways into the azygos
questions.explain: The bronchial circulation supplies oxygenated blood for the lung's metabolic needs, not for gas exchange.

questions.q: The bronchial arteries arise from which vessel?
questions.explain: Oxygenated blood flows into the bronchial arteries from the thoracic aorta to supply lung tissue and large airways.

items.why: Vagus: parasympathetic to pulmonary plexus -> bronchoconstriction, secretion

questions.q: Parasympathetic fibers carried to the pulmonary plexus by the vagus nerve cause which effect?
questions.explain: Vagal parasympathetic efferents cause bronchiolar muscle contraction, glandular secretion, and vasodilation; sympathetic fibers do the opposite.

items.why: Visceral vs parietal pleura; parietal senses pain (somatic), visceral does not; pneumothorax

questions.q: Which pleural layer can sense pain?
questions.explain: The parietal pleura has somatic innervation (intercostal and phrenic nerves) and senses pain; the visceral pleura has only visceral afferents.

questions.q: Loss of the negative pressure in the pleural space relative to the lung causes which condition?
questions.explain: The pleural space is held at negative pressure to keep the lung inflated; disrupting that pressure difference produces a pneumothorax (collapsed lung).

questions.q: Where does the visceral pleura become continuous with the parietal pleura?
questions.explain: The visceral pleura covers the lung and lines the fissures; at the hilum it is continuous with the parietal pleura lining the thoracic cavity.

items.why: Costodiaphragmatic recess: effusions collect here; blunted angle on x-ray

questions.q: On an upright chest x-ray, a pleural effusion first blunts the angle at which space?
questions.explain: Costal and diaphragmatic parietal pleura meet at the costodiaphragmatic recess, where pleural fluid accumulates and blunts the normally sharp angle.

items.why: Phrenic n. carries diaphragmatic parietal pleura pain (C3-C4) -> shoulder

questions.q: Irritation of the diaphragmatic parietal pleura causes pain referred to the shoulder. Which nerve carries the pleural pain?
questions.explain: Diaphragmatic parietal pleura pain travels via the phrenic nerve to C3-C4, which also supply the shoulder through supraclavicular nerves, so pain is referred there.

bricks.title: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles

items.why: Diaphragm: contracts down in inspiration; openings T8/T10/T12; inferior phrenic aa.; rises to T5

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the esophagus pass through the diaphragm?
questions.explain: 'I ate ten eggs at twelve': the IVC passes at T8, the esophagus at T10, and the aorta at T12.

questions.q: Which arteries provide the main blood supply to the diaphragm?
questions.explain: The diaphragm is supplied primarily from below by the inferior phrenic arteries, direct branches of the abdominal aorta.

questions.q: A chest tube must avoid the diaphragm and liver. Since the diaphragm can rise to T5 in expiration, it should go in which space?
questions.explain: During forced expiration the dome can move up to about T5, so a tube placed lower risks the abdomen; the 5th intercostal space or higher is used.

items.why: Phrenic n. (C3-C5): diaphragm motor + central sensory; trauma -> hemidiaphragm paralysis

questions.q: Which spinal cord segments give rise to the phrenic nerve?
questions.explain: Diaphragm motor innervation comes from C3, C4, and C5, which form the phrenic nerve.

questions.q: After neck trauma, a patient has paralysis of the left hemidiaphragm. Which nerve was most likely injured?
questions.explain: Each phrenic nerve supplies its own half of the diaphragm; phrenic nerve trauma is the most common cause of unilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis.

questions.q: Sensation from the peripheral diaphragm is carried by which nerves?
questions.explain: Sensation from the central diaphragm travels in the phrenic nerve, but the periphery is served by the intercostal and subcostal nerves.

items.why: Xiphoid: lowest sternum; anterior diaphragm attachment

questions.q: Anteriorly, the diaphragm attaches to which part of the sternum?
questions.explain: Anteriorly the diaphragm attaches to the bottom of the sternum, the xiphoid process.

items.why: True ribs 1-7 attach directly to sternum via own costal cartilages

questions.q: Which ribs are true ribs?
questions.explain: Ribs 1-7 articulate directly with the sternum via their own costal cartilages and are classified as true ribs.

items.why: False ribs 8-10: indirect via cartilage above; form costal margin

questions.q: Why are ribs 8-10 called false ribs?
choices: They have no anterior attachment at all
They reach the sternum via cartilage above
They do not articulate with vertebrae
Their cartilages join the xiphoid directly
questions.explain: Ribs 8, 9, and 10 articulate with the sternum only indirectly through the costal cartilages of the ribs above; they form the costal margin.

items.why: Floating ribs 11-12: no anterior attachment

questions.q: Which ribs are floating ribs?
questions.explain: Ribs 11 and 12 are floating ribs because they do not attach to the rest of the rib cage anteriorly.

items.why: Costal cartilages: rib-sternum link; diaphragm attaches to lowest 6 and their cartilages

questions.q: The costal part of the diaphragm attaches laterally to which structures?
choices: Upper six ribs and their costal cartilages
Lowest six ribs and costal cartilages
questions.explain: Laterally the diaphragm attaches directly to the lowest six ribs and their costal cartilages, forming its costal part.

items.why: Manubrium: upper sternum, meets body at sternal angle
Body of sternum: meets manubrium at sternal angle
Sternal angle: manubrium-body junction

questions.q: The sternal angle marks the junction of which two parts of the sternum?
questions.explain: The sternum consists of manubrium, body, and xiphoid process; the manubrium and body meet at the sternal angle.

items.why: Jugular notch: palpable midline landmark at superior sternum

questions.q: Which palpable midline landmark lies at the superior border of the sternum?
questions.explain: The jugular notch is a palpable midline landmark at the superior border of the sternum.

items.why: SC joint: clavicular notches of sternum with clavicles

questions.q: The sternoclavicular joint is formed by the clavicle and which sternal feature?
questions.explain: The clavicular notches of the sternum articulate with the clavicles to form the sternoclavicular joints.

items.why: Posterior intercostals: 1-2 from supreme intercostal, rest from aorta; costal groove

questions.q: The first and second posterior intercostal arteries arise from which vessel?
questions.explain: The first two posterior intercostals arise from the supreme intercostal artery off the costocervical trunk; the rest branch directly from the aorta.

questions.q: Where do the intercostal vessels run relative to each rib?
choices: Costal groove at the lower edge
Along the upper border of the rib
Deep to the parietal pleura only
questions.explain: The posterior and anterior intercostal vessels travel together beneath the lower edge of each rib in the costal groove.

items.why: Anterior intercostals: from internal thoracic, upper six spaces

questions.q: From which artery do the anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces arise?
questions.explain: Anterior intercostals branch from the internal thoracic artery and supply the upper six intercostal spaces.

items.why: Internal thoracic a.: anterior intercostals, musculophrenic; CABG graft

questions.q: Which artery is preferred for coronary bypass grafting because it resists atherosclerosis?
questions.explain: The internal thoracic artery is resistant to atherosclerosis, making it a reliable conduit for bypassing blocked coronary arteries.

questions.q: The musculophrenic artery, supplying intercostal spaces 7-9, is a terminal branch of which artery?
questions.explain: The musculophrenic artery, a terminal branch of the internal thoracic, supplies intercostal branches to the 7th-9th spaces.

items.why: External intercostals: elevate ribs in inspiration

questions.q: Which intercostal layer elevates the ribs to assist inspiration?
questions.explain: External intercostals run from the posterior aspect of one rib to the anterior aspect of the rib below, so their contraction elevates the ribs.

items.why: Internal intercostals: decrease thoracic volume in expiration

questions.q: Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles mainly does what?
choices: Elevates the ribs to increase thoracic volume
Lowers the dome of the diaphragm
Lifts the first rib in inspiration
questions.explain: Internal intercostals directly connect the ribs, so contraction shortens the distance between them and decreases thoracic volume during expiration.

items.why: Innermost intercostals assist internal intercostals in forced expiration

questions.q: The innermost intercostal muscles assist which other muscles, and in which phase?
questions.explain: Contraction of the innermost intercostals assists the internal intercostals during forced expiration.

items.why: Accessory: scalenes, pecs, SCM in forced inspiration; abdominal wall in forced expiration

questions.q: During an asthma attack, a patient's abdominal muscles contract with each breath. How do they help?
choices: Let the diaphragm contract fully downward
Push the diaphragm up in expiration
questions.explain: In respiratory distress the anterior abdominal wall muscles contract in forced expiration, pushing abdominal contents up against the diaphragm.

questions.q: Which muscle is an accessory muscle of forced inspiration?
questions.explain: The scalenes, pectoralis major and minor, and sternocleidomastoid elevate the rib cage in forced inspiration; abdominal muscles act in forced expiration.

questions.q: A patient in respiratory distress sits in the tripod position. Which muscles does this posture let help lift the chest wall?
questions.explain: In the tripod position, with arms fixed on the legs, the pectoralis muscles can lift the chest wall and assist inspiratory effort.

items.why: Intercostal nn. T1-T11 in costal groove (VAN); needle above the lower rib

questions.q: During thoracentesis, where should the needle enter to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle?
choices: Just below the lower border of the upper rib
Through the middle of the rib body
Just above the upper border of the lower rib
At the costal groove of the lower rib
questions.explain: The intercostal VAN runs in the costal groove along the inferior border of each rib, so the needle is inserted just above the upper border of the rib below.

questions.q: A needle placed too close to the inferior border of a rib injures the intercostal nerve. What is the most likely result?
questions.explain: Intercostal nerve injury causes sharp radiating chest wall pain, sensory loss, or paresthesia along the corresponding dermatome.

items.why: Thoracentesis at 7th-9th ICS midaxillary line to reach costodiaphragmatic recess

questions.q: Thoracentesis is most commonly done in the midaxillary line at which intercostal spaces to reach the costodiaphragmatic recess?
questions.explain: Thoracentesis is most commonly performed in the midaxillary line at the 7th-9th intercostal space to access the costodiaphragmatic recess.
